summary.text: The Humboldt Current, also called the Peru Current, is a cold, low-salinity current that flows north along the west coast of South America.
Upwelling brings nutrients to its surface, making it the most productive eastern boundary current system and the source of roughly 18–20% of the world's marine fish catch.
By cooling the sea air so it rarely makes rain, it is largely responsible for the dryness of the Atacama Desert and coastal Peru.

facts.label: Discovered by
facts.value: José de Acosta, 250 years before Humboldt

items.prompt: Near 5° south, in the tropics, the sea off Peru can be as cold as 16 °C. What keeps it so cold?

options.label: Cold, upwelled water carried north by a current
Meltwater pouring straight down from Andes glaciers
Cold mountain winds blowing far out over the sea
Icy springs leaking from the deep seafloor

items.explain: The current carries cold Sub-Antarctic water north, and cold, upwelled water reaches far up the coast.

items.prompt: The Atacama Desert sits right beside the ocean yet is extremely dry. How does the nearby current help?

options.label: It heats the air until rain evaporates
It pulls every cloud far out to sea
It cools sea air so it rarely rains
It makes the coastal soil too salty

items.explain: Marine air cooled by the current does not produce rain, though it can make clouds and fog.

items.prompt: The current bears Alexander von Humboldt's name. Was he the first to discover it?

options.label: Yes, on his voyage in the 1800s
No, someone found it 250 years earlier
No, Charles Darwin found it first
Yes, no sailor had ever noticed it before

items.explain: José de Acosta discovered it about 250 years before Humboldt; it was named after Humboldt anyway.

items.prompt: In some years an El Niño event reaches the coast of Peru. What happens to the system that feeds the fishery?

options.label: Upwelling gets stronger and catches boom
The current flows south for good
Nothing changes for the fish there
Upwelling is disrupted, hurting people

items.explain: El Niño periodically disrupts the upwelling behind the system's productivity, often with large social and economic impacts.

items.prompt: Under the surface lies a large zone with very little oxygen. Where does this push many organisms to stay?

options.label: Near the surface, for oxygen
Down on the deepest seafloor
Up coastal rivers in fresh water
Far out among Pacific islands

items.explain: The oxygen minimum zone forces many organisms to stay near the surface, where nutrients and oxygen are available.

items.prompt: Most fish caught in this current live in open water rather than on the bottom. Which catch fits?

options.label: Flounder and other flatfish
Crabs and spiny lobsters
Anchovies and sardines
Salmon and river trout

items.explain: The species are mostly pelagic, open-water fish: sardines, anchovies and jack mackerel.
